t.1.64.1: Then, having slain thousands of deer, the king with his ample train of mounts, intent on the pursuit of game, entered another forest.
t.1.64.2: All alone, he of supreme strength, overcome by hunger and thirst, reached the end of the forest and came upon a vast barren wasteland.
t.1.64.3: Having passed beyond that too, the king went on to another great forest, furnished with excellent hermitages, gladdening to the mind and exceedingly lovely to the eye, and filled with cool breezes.
t.1.64.4: It was strewn with flowering trees, exceedingly pleasant with its grassy meadows, vast, and likewise resounding with birds of sweet cries.
t.1.64.5: It was covered with trees whose branches had grown tall and whose shade was pleasant, its creepers swaying with bees, and it was endowed with the highest splendor.
t.1.64.6: In that forest there was no tree that was without flowers, none without fruit, none bearing thorns, nor any not swarmed over by bees.
t.1.64.7: The great archer entered a superb and delightful forest that resounded with birds and was richly adorned with flowers, its trees bearing blossoms of every season and its grassy meadows exceedingly pleasant.
t.1.64.8: There the trees, rich in blossoms and shaken by the wind, released again and again a many-colored shower of flowers.
t.1.64.9: Then the trees there shone forth, touching the sky, resounding with sweet-voiced birds, clothed in garments of variegated flowers.
t.1.64.10: There, on their young shoots bowed down by the weight of blossoms, birds together with bees utter a soft sound.
t.1.64.11: Seeing there many spots adorned with heaps of flowers, encircled by bowers of creepers and increasing the delight of the mind, that greatly splendid one then became joyful.
t.1.64.12: That forest shone with those trees, their branches intertwined with one another, heaped with blossoms, resembling the great banners of Indra.
t.1.64.13: The wind, pleasantly cool and fragrant, bearing the pollen of flowers, wandering about the trees in the forest, seemed to approach them with a longing for amorous play.
t.1.64.14: The king beheld that forest, endowed with such qualities, lovely, arising along the banks of a river, and resembling a raised banner.
t.1.64.15: But as he gazed upon that forest, full of joyful birds, he beheld a lovely and delightful hermitage, the finest of ashrams.
t.1.64.16: Strewn with trees of many kinds, its fires blazing brightly, surrounded by ascetics and Vālakhilyas, and attended by hosts of sages.
t.1.64.17: He saw it strewn with carpets of flowers, with its many fire-halls, and shining exceedingly with great, wide marshy thickets.
t.1.64.19: And the glorious great chariot-warrior arrived at that hermitage, which resembled the world of the gods and was exceedingly charming on every side.
t.1.64.20: He saw there a river of holy waters clinging close to the hermitage, standing like a mother to all living beings.
t.1.64.18: Near the holy river Mālinī, O king, with its pleasant waters, thronged with many flocks of birds and made lovely by its grove of ascetics, he saw even the beasts of prey grown gentle, and at the sight he was filled with delight.
t.1.64.21: He saw the river, its sandbanks thronged with cakravāka birds, its current bearing flowers and foam, a dwelling place for hosts of Kiṃnaras, and frequented by monkeys and bears.
t.1.64.23: Seeing the river bound up with the hermitage, and the hermitage grounds as well, the king then resolved to enter.
t.1.64.24: He entered the great forest, resounding with the cries of impassioned peacocks, adorned by the Mālinī, a river with islands and lovely banks, like the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa graced by the Gaṅgā.
t.1.64.22: It echoed with the sound of holy Vedic recitation, was adorned with sandy banks, and was frequented by rutting elephants, tigers and mighty serpents.
t.1.64.25: Then that lord of men, having approached that hermitage, which resembled Caitraratha, was exceedingly rich in excellent qualities and indescribable in its splendor, went to see the great seer Kaṇva, the descendant of Kaśyapa, whose wealth was austerity.
t.1.64.26: Having stationed at the entrance of the forest his army, full of chariots, crowded with horses and thronged with bands of foot soldiers, he spoke these words.
t.1.64.27: I shall go to see the sage Kāśyapa, the passionless one whose wealth is austerity. Remain here until my return.
t.1.64.28: Having reached that forest, which resembled Nandana, the king, lord of men, cast off his hunger and thirst and attained abundant joy.
t.1.64.29: Then that lord of men, accompanied by his ministers and with his family priest as companion, laid aside the insignia of royalty and went to that excellent hermitage, wishing to see there the imperishable seer, that heap of austerity.
t.1.64.30: And he, beholding the hermitage that resembled the world of Brahmā, resounding with the humming of bees and filled with flocks of birds of many kinds,
t.1.64.31: And that tiger among men heard the Ṛg verses being recited by the foremost of the Bahvṛcas with the pada and krama methods, while the sacrificial rites were being performed here.
t.1.64.32: That hermitage then shone with men versed in sacrifice, in the sciences and their auxiliary limbs, and with those who recited the Vedic texts in their krama sequences, men of boundless spirit and strict self-restraint.
t.1.64.34: Resounding with other twice-born ones speaking words endowed with grammatical refinement, that glorious hermitage shone like the world of Brahmā.
t.1.64.33: And there, O sacrificer, the foremost knowers of the Atharvaveda, esteemed by the assemblies, recited the Saṃhitā together with its pada and krama readings.
t.1.64.35: It was thronged by those who knew sacrifice and the sacred rites, by men skilled in the krama recitation and in phonetics, by those endowed with knowledge of the true meaning of logic, and by masters of the Vedas.
t.1.64.38: And here and there the slayer of enemy heroes saw the foremost of brahmins, self-restrained and firm in their vows, devoted to muttered prayer and fire-offerings, perfected ones.
t.1.64.36: It was filled with men skilled in combining and correlating diverse statements, who knew the particular duties to be performed and were wholly devoted to the dharma of liberation.
t.1.64.39: Seeing the wonderful seats strewn with flowers, carefully arranged, the lord of the earth was filled with amazement.
t.1.64.37: And it echoed on every side with the foremost Lokāyatikas, who had gained a true grasp of establishing a thesis, raising objections, and reaching the final conclusion.
t.1.64.40: And seeing the worship of the shrines of the gods performed by the twice-born, that best of kings deemed himself to be dwelling in the world of Brahmā.
t.1.64.41: He could not have his fill of gazing upon that splendid, excellent hermitage, protected by the austerities of Kāśyapa and filled with hosts of ascetics rich in penance.
t.1.64.42: That slayer of foes, together with his ministers and his family priest, entered the hermitage of Kāśyapa, surrounded on all sides by seers of great vows whose wealth was austerity, a secluded, exceedingly charming and auspicious place.
